### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives (Week 12)

- **Explain** how text, audio, images and video are converted to numbers.
- **Run** small demonstrations of each data type using only base R.

> 📌 NUC course contents covered this week: *"Use cases in various domains such as Image, Natural Language, Audio and Video."*

---

## 1. Text: From Sentences to Numbers

Computers cannot read words; they count them. The first step is **tokenisation**: splitting text into words.

```{r text}
review <- c("The delivery was fast and the packaging was good",
            "Packaging was poor and delivery was slow",
            "Good price and fast delivery")

tokens <- strsplit(tolower(review), "[^a-z]+")
words  <- unlist(tokens)
sort(table(words), decreasing = TRUE)        # word frequencies (a bag of words)
```

A tiny sentiment score using word lists:

```{r sentiment}
positive <- c("good", "fast")
negative <- c("poor", "slow")
score <- sapply(tokens, function(w) sum(w %in% positive) - sum(w %in% negative))
data.frame(review = review, sentiment = score)
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 1:** Add three reviews of your own (one in Pidgin or Yorùbá if you wish). What happens with the phrase "not good"? Why do real systems need more than word lists?

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
*Worked answer.* "not good" contains the positive word "good", so the word-list score is +1 although the meaning is negative. A word list ignores word order and negation. Real systems use context (n-grams or contextual embeddings from language models), and for low-resource languages such as Yorùbá, Hausa and Igbo there is far less training text, so models perform worse.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

---

## 2. Audio: A Waveform Is a Sequence of Numbers

Sound is pressure over time. We **sample** it: measure the amplitude many times per second (the sampling rate).

```{r audio}
fs   <- 8000                                  # samples per second
t    <- seq(0, 0.01, by = 1 / fs)             # 10 milliseconds
wave <- sin(2 * pi * 440 * t)                 # a 440 Hz tone (musical note A4)

plot(t, wave, type = "l", xlab = "Time (s)", ylab = "Amplitude", main = "440 Hz tone")
length(wave)                                   # number of samples in 10 ms
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 2:** Change the frequency to 880 Hz. How many full cycles fit in 0.01 s?

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
```{r audio-solution}
# cycles = frequency x duration
440 * 0.01   # 4.4 cycles
880 * 0.01   # 8.8 cycles: doubling the frequency doubles the cycles (one octave higher)
```
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

---

## 3. Images: A Picture Is a Matrix

A grayscale image is a grid of numbers from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A colour image has three such grids (red, green, blue).

```{r image}
img <- matrix(0, 8, 8)
img[3:6, 3:6] <- 255                           # a bright square
img <- img + matrix(rnorm(64, 0, 20), 8, 8)    # add noise
image(t(img[8:1, ]), col = gray.colors(256), axes = FALSE, main = "A noisy 8 x 8 image")

mean(img > 128)                                 # share of bright pixels
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 3:** Make the square smaller and increase the noise (`sd = 80`). Can you still see it? What does this say about image quality and model accuracy?

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
With strong noise the signal-to-noise ratio falls and the square disappears, and a classifier trained on clean images would fail on noisy ones. In practice, photos taken on low-quality phones in poor light (for example cassava leaves in the field) must be represented in the training data.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

---

## 4. Video: A Sequence of Images

```{r video}
frames <- lapply(1:5, function(i) { m <- matrix(0, 8, 8); m[3:6, i:(i + 1)] <- 255; m })
sapply(frames, mean)                            # average brightness per frame

# Motion: the difference between consecutive frames is non-zero where something moved
moved <- sapply(2:5, function(i) sum(frames[[i]] != frames[[i - 1]]))
moved
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 4:** What would the `moved` vector look like for a video of an empty road? How could this idea be used to count vehicles?

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
All zeros: nothing changes between frames. Counting vehicles can start from frame differencing (find the regions that change) followed by tracking each region across frames; modern systems use deep-learning object detectors instead.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

## 5. Course Review: Check Your Answers in R

Work each problem by hand first, then compare with R.

```{r review}
# 1. A coin lands heads 118 times in 200 tosses: is it fair?
binom.test(118, 200)

# 2. Regression of score on hours
hours <- c(2, 4, 6, 8); score <- c(50, 60, 75, 85)
fit <- lm(score ~ hours)
coef(fit)
predict(fit, data.frame(hours = 5))

# 3. Basket measures: 500 baskets, 100 rice, 80 oil, 60 both
n <- 500; rice <- 100; oil <- 80; both <- 60
c(support = both / n, confidence = both / rice, lift = (both / rice) / (oil / n))
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 5:** Write one practice question for each of Weeks 1 to 12 and its R answer.

### Revision checklist

- [ ] I can classify datasets as structured, semi-structured or unstructured.
- [ ] I can list and explain the steps of the data science process.
- [ ] I can compute and interpret mean, standard deviation and correlation.
- [ ] I can simulate a coin or die and explain the law of large numbers.
- [ ] I can fit and interpret a simple regression and compute MSE.
- [ ] I can compute support, confidence and lift and interpret clusters.
- [ ] I can state H0 and H1, read a p-value and report an effect size.
- [ ] I can explain BI, KPIs, ETL, the 5 Vs and the DIKW pyramid.
- [ ] I can read, change and run a short R script.
